newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Rich, powerful Korean unions battle labour law.
newsitem.headline: Rich, powerful Korean unions battle labour law.

text.p: Before Hyundai Motor Co workers had a union, martial arts experts dished out military-style discipline on factory floors and company guards with hair clippers enforced a short back-and-sides rule.
Now the union often calls the shots at South Korea's biggest car works in the southeast city of Ulsan -- and the company must pay its 42 full-time officers.
"They are very scared of us," said union official Yoon Jong-o.

Hyundai workers were at the front line of strikes that crippled the auto industry after the ruling party last month rammed through parliament a law to emasculate unions that were born in 1987 and have grown into formiddable giants.
The government has partially backed down, throwing the legislation back to parliament for debate.
But anger is still simmering among unionists who want the law scrapped altogether.
Few believe the government wants to turn back the clock to brutal management practises that led to an explosion of worker anger after 1987.
One of the first victories of the Hyundai union was to secure the right for workers to grow their hair a bit longer.

Clippers in hand, guards at the factory gates would grab workers as they streamed in and out of the plant and shear their hair to a bristle. The indignity rankled more than being watched over by experts in "taekwondo", a Korean martial art.
"When we first formed our union, one of our top requests to mangement was freedom of hairstyle," recalled Yoon.
Money is not the central issue now with Hyundai workers, who are probably better off than their British counterparts.

Production line workers with 10 years experience can earn around $28,000 each year and are eligible for a host of benefits from subsidised housing to free medical care and schooling. Annual holiday entitlement is six weeks.
Nor is the union very concerned about job security, even though the new law makes it easier for companies to sack workers and hire temporary employees.
"We don't worry too much about layoffs," said Yoon.

Instead, Yoon is more worried about the impact of the legislation on his union organisation, which occupies a whole floor of a company administration block and commands a war chest of $5 million built up through member subscriptions.
Among other provisions, the law would make it illegal for companies to pay full-time union staff.
The bill, in its present form, also maintains a ban on the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, to which Hyundai unions are affiliated.
The Hyundai Motor union represents 20,000 of the 29,000-strong workforce, and has the cash flow of a modest-sized company. It budgets about $700,000 each year for rallies and protest meetings.
Some of its largesse is handed back to members in the form of gifts to mark the anniversary of the union's birth. This year it was an ice-box, last year a clock.

And to cultivate respect in the community, it organises parties at old people's homes and is active in civic affairs, such as traffic control. It has ambitions of funding politicians to run for national office.

Hyundai management has bought the computers, facsimile machines and photocopiers that keep union offices humming. It even supplies space used by the union to store drums beaten during strikes to disrupt work.
And the company foots the annual $1.2 million wage bill for the 42 full-time officers.
Union members pay one percent of their salary each year to the union, giving it an annual income of $3.5 million.
